text: Every application is built for human interaction, with pages, menus, forms, and controls that become obstacles for agents.
Pages, menus, filters, accounts, and forms are translations between one human intention and one provider action.
Providers pay the same tax: frontend and backend workflows for every interaction they can predict.
Our goal is to replace that application-specific interaction code with reasoning at runtime.
Many websites optimize navigation and attention even when the user already knows the result they want.
If an agent understands the same human actions, the interaction no longer needs to be pre-rendered as pages and forms.
For example, booking a flight still means navigating filters, seat maps, and checkout.
The changing workflow can come from LLM reasoning instead of permanently written application logic.
For example, reasoning can rebook disrupted travel without a prewritten recovery flow.
A small trusted substrate remains for identity, permission, storage, validation, and transport.
The user describes a difficult real outcome once and supplies the context the model needs.
The LLM reasons visually about the apartment, detects accessibility problems, and preserves every personal constraint.
It discovers ramp rental, moving, equipment, delivery, installation, and building-rule capabilities by meaning.
Those independent providers are composed into one plan; the agent asks only for decisions that require consent.
The output is the adapted plan and verified commitments — not six websites, directories, calendars, and checkout forms.
No provider could predict this exact workflow. The LLM creates it through reasoning for this person and this moment.
Websites and mobile apps encode actions in permanent human-operated interfaces.
APIs remove the visual layer, but developers still hand-code every connection and workflow.
Chatbots and browser agents usually sit on top of the same flows; generative UI creates another interface.
Provider worlds describe capabilities, rules, and state in natural language, so agents can reason over them and invoke any action without hard-coded business logic.
The prototype uses generated HTML as a bridge. The final direction removes that temporary interface too.
The model should reason from request to result instead of generating software that the user must operate.
Before, every expected outcome needs an application-specific workflow stack built in advance.
That stack includes routes, forms, state, branches, provider adapters, result views, and the libraries connecting them.
Each new journey adds implementation, testing, dependencies, and maintenance before the user can request it.
The benefit is adaptability: one reasoning process can combine context, constraints, capabilities, and live state for outcomes no developer preprogrammed.
This removes repeated workflow code and lets providers add capabilities once, while deterministic systems still enforce permission, validation, storage, and execution.
Context tells the model who the user is, what is happening now, and which constraints must survive the plan.
Tools let the agent discover capabilities, retrieve live information, perform authorized operations, and verify results.
Memory carries useful preferences and previous decisions forward without making the user repeat them.
Together they allow more application-specific frontend and backend workflow code to become runtime reasoning.
The end goal is an internet where people communicate desired outcomes and generative AI returns the result directly.
The primary question is whether one shared reasoning runtime can serve different intents without a separately implemented workflow for each one.
The simple baseline assumes a prebuilt route, form, workflow branches, provider handlers, and result view for every journey.
The agent uses the same configured runtime and generic invocation contract across all four fixed evaluation intents.
In the documented live run, generated experiences were returned for zero of four baseline cases and four of four agent cases.
This shows the runtime can create task-specific experiences; verified real-world completion remains the next measure.
Semantic discovery is supporting evidence: relevant top-provider ranking improved from two of four to four of four fixed cases.
Average human actions fall from three point seven five to two, but those values are modeled assumptions, not observed telemetry.
Integration tests separately verify a two-provider plan, a state update with a decision event, and duplicate-action suppression.
The evidence supports replacing more task-specific workflow implementation with reasoning, while trusted execution systems remain.
We started from the simple baseline: every expected journey needs its own route, form, branches, integrations, and result view.
The first experiment replaced those per-intent screens with one shared runtime, generated experiences, and a generic action bridge.
Malformed model output and browser failures taught us to replace direct parsing with validation, fallback, error capture, and repair.
Semantic discovery fixed vocabulary mismatch, improving relevant top-provider ranking from two of four to four of four fixed cases.
Composition then combined two separate services into one tested plan and one user-facing experience.
The final evaluation shows the overall gain and its limits: generated UI is today’s bridge, while direct verified results are the next experiment.
